subject: ENGL101
title: Unit 3: Basic Principles in Medicine + Digestive, Respiratory, and Circulatory Systems

A.q: What is physiology?
options: Study of the body functions and organs
Study of the body structure and bones
Study of the disease processes and cells
Study of the external body and shape
A.explain: Physiology is the study of the functions of the body and its internal organs. Structure is anatomy. Disease processes and external shape are not the definition.

A.q: What is anatomy?
options: Study of the structure of the body
Study of the functions of the body
Study of the chemical body cell processes
Study of the disease and its symptoms
A.explain: Anatomy is the study of the structure of the body. Functions are physiology. Chemical processes and disease symptoms are other areas.

A.q: Match each body system to its main job.

rightItems.text: Brings in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide
Breaks down food and absorbs nutrients
Supports the body and protects organs

A.explain: Cardiovascular pumps blood to all parts. Respiratory inhales and exhales using the nose, trachea, lungs, and diaphragm. Digestive breaks down food; the colon reabsorbs water and forms feces. Skeletal supports, protects, and aids movement. Muscular moves by contracting and relaxing. Nervous sends electrical signals.

A.q: Match each body system to its main job.

rightItems.text: Covers and protects the body surface

A.explain: Endocrine releases hormones and controls metabolism. Lymphatic returns fluid, rids toxins, and fights infection. Integumentary is the skin and hair that protect the surface. Urinary filters waste and excess water. Reproductive produces offspring.

A.q: What is bone made up of?
A.explain: Bone is a living growing tissue made up of water, collagen, and minerals such as calcium phosphate. Blood cells are in blood. Muscle fibers and tendons are soft tissue. Air and fluid alone do not form bone.

A.q: What do arteries do?
options: Carry blood away from the heart
Carry blood back to the heart
A.explain: Arteries carry blood away from the heart to other body parts and tissues. They are very muscular and elastic. Veins carry blood back. Capillaries allow exchange. Heart chambers are atria and ventricles.

A.q: What do veins do?
options: Carry blood back to the heart
Carry blood away from the heart
A.explain: Veins carry blood back from other body parts. Their walls are thinner than arteries. Arteries carry blood away. Capillaries exchange nutrients. Platelets help clotting.

A.q: What are platelets?
options: Small cells involved in the blood clotting
Large cells that carry oxygen in the blood
White cells that fight off body infections
Hard cells forming the tissue in the bones
A.explain: Platelets are a small disc-shaped cell found in large numbers in blood and involved in clotting. Red blood cells carry oxygen. White blood cells fight infection. Bone cells form tissue.

A.q: What is a nutrient?
options: Substance used to survive grow and reproduce
Main protein found inside skin and bone
Small vessel that exchanges the blood nutrients
Smallest basic unit of the human life
A.explain: A nutrient is a substance used by an organism to survive, grow, and reproduce. Collagen is the protein in skin and bone. Capillary is the exchange vessel. Cell is the smallest unit of life.

A.q: What is the heart?
options: Organ that pumps blood around the body
Vessel that returns blood to the heart
Tissue made of water and collagen
A.explain: The heart is an organ which pumps blood around the body. Ribs protect the lungs. Vein returns blood. Bone tissue is made of water and collagen.

A.q: How many chambers does the heart have?
A.explain: The heart has two atria and two ventricles. The other counts are wrong: it never has one atrium with three ventricles, nor two atria with one or three ventricles.

A.q: What are vertebrae?
options: Small bones connected to form the spine
Large bones that form the human pelvis
Small vessels that carry the human blood
Tiny cells that help the blood to clot
A.explain: The vertebrae are the small bones that are connected to form the spine. Pelvis is the large bony frame. Vessels carry blood. Platelets help clotting.

A.q: What is collagen?
options: Main protein found in skin and bone
Main element in food needed for health
Main vessel that exchanges the nutrients
Smallest basic unit of the human life
A.explain: Collagen is the main protein found in skin and bone. Nutrient is the food element. Capillary exchanges nutrients. Cell is the smallest unit.

A.q: What is the anatomical position?
options: Standing erect with palms facing forward
Lying flat with arms crossed on the chest
Sitting upright with head tilted backward
Standing straight with palms facing back
A.explain: Anatomical position is standing erect, facing observer, head level, eyes forward, feet flat pointing forward, hands at sides with palms facing forwards. Other postures do not match.

A.q: What does anterior mean?
options: Toward the front of the body
Toward the back of the body
A.explain: Anterior means toward the front. Posterior is toward the back. Superior is toward the head. Inferior is toward the feet.

A.q: What does posterior mean?
options: Toward the back of the body
Toward the front of the body
A.explain: Posterior means toward the back. Anterior is toward the front. Medial is toward the center. Lateral is toward the sides.

A.q: What does superior mean?
A.explain: Superior means above or toward the head. Inferior means below or toward the feet. Anterior is front. Posterior is back.

A.q: What does inferior mean?
A.explain: Inferior means below or toward the feet. Superior is above or toward the head. Medial is toward the center. Superficial is toward the surface.

A.q: What does medial mean?
options: Nearer to the center of the body
Farther from the center of the body
Toward the surface of the human body
Away from the surface of the human body
A.explain: Medial means nearer to the center or median plane. Lateral is farther from the center. Superficial is toward the surface. Deep is away from the surface.

A.q: What does proximal mean?
options: Nearer to the attachment of a limb
Farther from the attachment of a limb
A.explain: Proximal means nearer to the attachment of a limb to the trunk. Distal means farther away. Superior is toward the head. Inferior is toward the feet.

A.q: What does distal mean?
options: Farther from the attachment of a limb
Nearer to the attachment of a limb
Toward the surface of the human body
Away from the surface of the human body
A.explain: Distal means farther away from the attachment of a limb. Proximal is nearer. Superficial is toward the surface. Deep is away from the surface.

A.q: What does superficial mean?
options: Toward the surface of the body
Away from the surface of the body
A.explain: Superficial means toward the surface of the body. Deep means away from the surface. Medial is toward the center. Posterior is toward the back.

A.q: What does deep mean?
options: Away from the surface of the body
Toward the surface of the human body
Nearer to the center of the body
Farther from the center of the body
A.explain: Deep means away from the surface of the body. Superficial is toward the surface. Medial is nearer to the center. Lateral is farther from the center.

A.q: Match each structure pair to the direction of the first relative to the second.

leftItems.text: Heart relative to the vertebral column

A.explain: The sternum is anterior to the lungs and the heart is anterior to the spine, which runs down the back. The heart is superior to the stomach and the neck superior to the chest. The abdomen and the ventricles are inferior, and the lungs are posterior to the breastbone. Proximal and distal fit none.

A.q: What separates the thorax from the abdomen?
A.explain: The diaphragm separates the thorax from the abdomen. Sternum is the breastbone. Pelvis is the bony frame. Vertebrae form the spine.

A.q: What does the frontal plane divide the body into?
A.explain: The frontal plane passes through both ears, dividing the body into two vertical parts: front versus back. Lateral/sagittal divides left and right. Transverse divides top and bottom.

A.q: What does the transverse plane divide the body into?
A.explain: The transverse plane passes through the waist, dividing the body horizontally from top to bottom. Frontal is front and back. Lateral/sagittal is left and right.

A.q: What protects the heart and the lungs?
A.explain: The ribs form the cage that protects the heart and the lungs. The vertebrae stack into the spine at the back. The tendons link muscles to bones. The ligaments link bones at the joints.

A.q: What does the word collapse mean?
A.explain: To collapse is to fall down or give way. To get larger is to expand, the opposite of coming down. To stand upright is to stay erect, what a structure does before it collapses. To move around is to change place, not to come down.

A.q: Why do bones weaken as a person gets older?
options: Body makes too many red cells
A.explain: Bones weaken because minerals start to disappear from the bones. Muscle size, red cell production, and water uptake are not the stated reason.

A.q: What is the primary purpose of ligaments?
A.explain: Ligaments connect bones together at the joints. They are strong and can stretch. Producing blood cells, shielding the brain, and storing minerals are other bone functions.

A.q: What is the function of tendons?
A.explain: Tendons link muscles to bones. Ligaments link bones together. Stretching is a property of ligaments. Protection is not the stated function.

A.q: Approximately how many bones does an adult human have?
A.explain: An adult has about 206 bones. A newborn has roughly 270 to 300 bones that fuse during growth.

A.q: Match each combining form to what it means.
A.explain: Cardio- means heart and gastro- means stomach, as in cardiovascular, cardiologist, and gastroenteritis. Body is physi-, excess is hyper-, and again is re-.

A.q: Match each prefix to what it means.
A.explain: Hyper- means excess, physi- means body, and re- means again. Inside is in-, before is pre-, not is un-, and pertaining to is -ic or -ous.

A.q: What is the opposite of the verb protect?
A.explain: The opposite of protect is to hurt. To guard, to shield, and to defend all mean to keep something safe, the same idea as protect, so none of them is the opposite.

A.q: Where is the thigh bone located?
options: In the upper part of the leg
At the top of the human collarbone
Near the front of the human shoulder
Above the base of the human pelvis
A.explain: The upper part of the leg is the thigh bone. It forms part of the knee. Collarbone and shoulder are in the arm. Pelvis connects the leg to the spine.

A.q: What is a cell?
options: The smallest basic unit of life
A primary component of the blood
A lower chamber of the heart
A major vessel of the blood
A.explain: A cell is the smallest unit of life. Platelet is a blood component. Ventricle is a heart chamber. Vein is a blood vessel.

A.q: What is a ventricle?
options: Right or left chamber of the heart
Vessel that returns blood to the heart
Main component found in the human blood
Protein found in the skin and bone
A.explain: A ventricle is the right or left chamber of the heart. Vein returns blood. Platelet is a blood component. Collagen is the protein.

A.q: What does gastrointestinal mean?
options: Relating to the stomach and intestines
Relating to the heart and blood vessels
Relating to the skin and outer surface
Relating to the bones and skeletal frame
A.explain: Gastrointestinal relates to the stomach and intestines. Cardiovascular relates to heart and vessels. Superficial relates to surface. Skeletal relates to bones.

A.q: Which group names blood vessels only?
A.explain: The arteries, veins, and capillaries are all blood vessels. The bones, cartilage, and ligaments belong to the skeleton and its connections. The muscles, tendons, and joints belong to movement. The cells, tissues, and organs are levels of body organization, not vessels.

A.q: What is the forearm?
options: Part of the arm between elbow and wrist
Part of the leg between knee and ankle
Part of the trunk between chest and pelvis
Part of the head between eyes and chin
A.explain: The forearm is the part of the arm between the elbow and the wrist. Lower leg is between knee and ankle. Trunk includes chest abdomen and pelvis.

A.q: What is the pelvis?
options: Large bony frame at the base of spine
Small connected bones that form the human spine
Hard protective bone that covers the human brain
Long bone between the elbow and the wrist
A.explain: The pelvis is the large bony frame near the base of the spine. Vertebrae form the spine. Skull protects the brain. Forearm is between elbow and wrist.

A.q: What is a capillary?
options: Vessels that return blood to the heart
Vessels that carry blood from the heart
Cells that are involved in blood clotting
A.explain: A capillary is a vessel permitting the exchange of nutrients. Vein returns blood. Artery carries blood away. Platelet is involved in clotting.

A.q: What does lateral mean?
options: Located on one side of the body
Located much nearer to the body center
Located toward the front of the body
Located toward the back of the body
A.explain: Lateral is a location on one side of the body or an organ. Medial is nearer the center. Anterior is front. Posterior is back.

A.q: Which imperative fits: ______ the full dose of IV antibiotics?
A.explain: Administer the full dose of IV antibiotics. Elevate is for a limb. Sterilize is for equipment. Wash is for hands or wounds.

A.q: What is the most appropriate action if a patient shows signs of an allergic reaction to a medication?
options: Discontinue the medication immediately and notify the doctor
Administer another dose to counteract the bad symptoms
Monitor the patient closely without changing anything else
Help the patient change position to relieve their discomfort
A.explain: Discontinue the medication immediately if the patient has any signs of an allergic reaction, such as a rash. Administer starts the dose. Monitor checks signs. Help is for positioning.

A.q: Into how many main regions is the human body divided?
A.explain: The body has five main regions: head, neck, trunk, upper limbs, lower limbs. 'It has four main regions' undercounts. 'It has seven main regions' and 'It has eight main regions' overcount.

A.q: Match each limb or region to the point where it attaches to the trunk.
A.explain: The neck joins the head to the trunk, the shoulder joins the upper limbs, and the groin joins the lower limbs. The waist is a trunk band, while the trunk and back are not join points.

A.q: Match each body region to the parts that make it up.

rightItems.text: Shoulders, arms, forearms, wrists, and hands

A.explain: The upper limbs are the shoulders, arms, forearms, wrists, and hands. The lower limbs are the buttocks, legs, ankles, and feet. The trunk is the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. The line 'Shoulders, arms, and buttocks' mixes upper- and lower-limb parts, so it matches no single region.

A.q: Match each structure pair to how the first sits relative to the second.
A.explain: The trachea is on the neck midline, so it is medial to the lungs; the arms hang at the sides, so they are lateral to the trunk. The elbow is nearer the attachment than the hand (proximal) and farther from the torso than the shoulder (distal). Superficial and deep fit none.

A.q: Match each description to the correct name.
A.explain: The breastbone is the sternum, the spine is the backbone, and the thorax is the chest. The skeleton is the framework of bones and cartilage, and the disk is the cushion between vertebrae. Collarbone matches none of these.

A.q: Which flat bone is located on the back of the shoulder?
A.explain: The shoulder blade is the flat bone on the back of the shoulder. The breastbone is the sternum, the pelvis is near the base of the spine, and the collarbone is at the front of the shoulder area.

A.q: In the cardiovascular vocabulary list, pump means to move or ___ around.
A.explain: Pump means to move or push something around. In the cardiovascular system, the heart pumps blood by pushing it around the body. Break, filter, and protect do not match the meaning of pump.

A.q: Bone is described as a living, growing...
A.explain: Bone is described as a living, growing tissue made of water, collagen, and minerals. It is not an organ system, vessel, or heart chamber.

A.q: What does ingest mean?
options: Take food or drink into the body
Examine the stomach with an instrument
A.explain: Ingest means to take food or drink into the body by swallowing or absorbing. Removing waste is elimination, pumping blood is circulation, and examining the stomach relates to gastroscope.

A.q: Intake is an amount of food, air, or another substance ___.
A.explain: Intake refers to an amount of food, air, or another substance taken into the body. The liver produces bile, veins carry blood, and kidneys filter waste, but none of these define intake.

A.q: What does internal mean?
A.explain: Internal means on the inside. Toward the back is posterior.

A.q: Physiotherapy treats disease or injury mainly through ___.
options: physical methods such as massage and exercise
drug treatments such as antibiotics and painkillers
surgical procedures such as transplants and biopsies
chemical treatments such as medicines and injections
A.explain: Physiotherapy uses physical methods such as massage and exercise to treat disease or injury. Drugs, surgery, and diagnostic tools belong to other areas of medical treatment or examination.

A.q: What does renew mean?
options: Breathe at an abnormally fast rate
A.explain: Renew means to restart or make new again. Hyperventilate means to breathe abnormally fast, gastro- relates to the stomach, and the immune system protects from infection.

A.q: What does reshape mean?
options: Examine the interior of the stomach
A.explain: Reshape means to form again. Moving blood is pumping, filtering waste relates to the urinary system, and examining the stomach relates to a gastroscope.

A.q: Gastroenteritis is inflammation of the ___.
A.explain: Gastroenteritis means inflammation of the stomach and intestines. The other pairs name digestive structures whose inflammation carries different terms, not gastroenteritis.

A.q: A gastroscope is an instrument used to examine the ___.
A.explain: A gastroscope is an instrument used to examine the stomach. The gallbladder is typically viewed with ultrasound, the small intestine with an enteroscope, and the colon with a colonoscope.

A.q: Hypertension is a medical term for ___.
A.explain: Hypertension means high blood pressure. High blood sugar is hyperglycemia, excessive muscle tension is not a standard term for hypertension, and elevated body temperature relates to hyperthermia.

A.q: Hyperglycemic describes an excess of ___ in the bloodstream.
A.explain: Hyperglycemic describes an excess of glucose in the bloodstream. Hyper- means excess, and glycemic relates to sugar or glucose.

A.q: Hyperventilate means to breathe ___.
A.explain: Hyperventilate means to breathe at an abnormally fast rate. Hyper- suggests excess or high, and ventilate relates to breathing. Abnormally slowly, at high pressure, and through the mouth do not match the meaning.

A.q: The female reproductive organs include the ovaries, the uterus, the vagina, and the ___.
A.explain: The female reproductive organs include the ovaries, uterus, vagina, and fallopian tubes. The urinary bladder and urethral opening are urinary structures. The scrotum is a male reproductive structure.

A.q: Diarrhea and ___ are classic symptoms of gastroenteritis.
A.explain: Diarrhea and vomiting are classic symptoms of gastroenteritis, which is inflammation of the stomach and intestines. Coughing and sneezing are more related to respiratory irritation, and blushing is a facial reddening response.

A.q: The lateral or sagittal plane divides the body into which parts?
A.explain: The lateral or sagittal plane divides the body vertically into left and right parts. The frontal plane divides front and back, and the transverse plane divides top and bottom.

A.q: Which structure protects the brain?
A.explain: The skull protects the brain. The ribs protect the heart and lungs, the pelvis supports the lower trunk, and the sternum is the breastbone.

A.q: Bones store minerals and release them into the ___.
A.explain: Bones store minerals needed by the body. When minerals are required, they are released into the blood.

A.q: Bones also form new red and white ___ each day.
A.explain: Bones form new red and white blood cells each day. Glands, vessels, and fibers are not the cells formed in bones.

A.q: A joint is the place where two ___ come together.
A.explain: A joint is the place where two bones come together. Muscles move bones, tendons attach muscles to bones, and organs are body structures.

A.q: Which is the biggest and strongest joint in the body?
A.explain: The knee joint is described as the biggest and strongest joint in the body.

A.q: The vertebrae are hollow, and ___ run down through them.
A.explain: The vertebrae are hollow, and nerves run down through the hollow parts to the rest of the body.

A.q: Arm bones are connected at the top to the collarbone and the ___ bone.
A.explain: Arm bones are connected at the top to the collarbone and the shoulder bone. The thigh and pelvic bones belong to the lower limb region, and ribs belong to the chest.

A.q: Bones are living cells that grow and ___ over time.
A.explain: Bones are living cells. They grow and change over time. Collapse, digest, and breathe are not functions of bone cells.

A.q: A new bone is still made until a person reaches about age ___.
A.explain: New bone is still made until about age 35, after which bones gradually weaken. The figures 60, 25, and 20 are not the age bone formation stops.

A.q: In 'the bones include the ribs and skull', include means ___.
A.explain: Include means contain. The bones contain or have parts such as the ribs and skull.

A.q: In 'bones are necessary for movement', necessary means ___.
A.explain: Necessary means needed or important. Bones are needed for movement, support, and protection.

A.q: Gastric juices help turn the bolus into a thick what?
A.explain: Gastric juices help turn the bolus into a thick liquid. Solid, gas, and powder do not describe the resulting mixture in the stomach.

A.q: Match each digestive organ to what it does.

rightItems.text: Grinds food and forms the bolus
Moistens food to ease chewing and swallowing
Mixes food and molds the bolus
Moves the bolus down to the stomach
Stores food and churns it into chyme
Stores bile until digestion needs it
Breaks food into simple soluble substances

A.explain: The mouth grinds food into a bolus; the salivary glands moisten it; the tongue mixes and molds it. The esophagus moves it to the stomach, which stores and churns it into chyme. The liver secretes bile and the gallbladder stores it; the pancreas breaks food into simple soluble substances. The small intestine absorbs nutrients, the large intestine reabsorbs water and forms feces, the rectum holds feces, and the anus expels them.

A.q: Match each process to its description.

rightItems.text: Process of breaking down food into nutrients
When solid waste leaves the body
When nutrients pass into the blood
When food passes from the mouth to the stomach

A.explain: Digestion is the process of breaking down food into nutrients. Elimination is when solid waste leaves the body. Absorption is when nutrients pass into the blood. Ingestion is when food passes from the mouth to the stomach. Storing water only fits none of these.

A.q: Which structure is used for both eating and breathing?
A.explain: The pharynx connects the mouth to the esophagus and the nose to the trachea, so it serves both eating and breathing. The esophagus carries food, the trachea carries air, and the larynx is the voice box in the airway.

A.q: The esophagus is a muscular tube that connects the pharynx with the ______.
A.explain: The esophagus is a muscular tube connecting the pharynx to the stomach, and it moves food toward the stomach. The liver makes bile, the small intestine absorbs nutrients, and the lung is respiratory. Waste leaves through the anus later.

A.q: Which digestive structure is a bag that stores food?
A.explain: The stomach is a bag-like organ where food is stored. The esophagus moves food, the liver secretes bile, and the gallbladder stores bile.

A.q: The respiratory system's main function is to supply oxygen to all parts of the body through breathing: inhaling oxygen-rich air and exhaling air filled with what?
A.explain: The respiratory system supplies oxygen and exhales air filled with carbon dioxide, a waste gas. Nitrogen gas, water vapor, and fresh oxygen do not describe the primary exhaled waste.

A.q: When we breathe in, air enters which structure?
A.explain: When we breathe in, air enters the nose. The anus, stomach, and liver are not the entry for inhaled air.

A.q: In the lungs, oxygen passes from the air into the blood through which structures?
A.explain: In the lungs, oxygen passes from the air into the blood through the alveoli. Bronchi, trachea, and diaphragm are other respiratory structures but not the site of gas exchange.

A.q: The blood picks up which gas from body cells?
A.explain: The blood picks up carbon dioxide from body cells. Oxygen is delivered to cells. Nitrogen and bile are not the gas picked up from cells.

A.q: Match each term to its description.

rightItems.text: Long tube that takes air from the mouth to the bronchi
Flat muscle that pulls and pushes the lungs
Tiny air sacs with thin walls to exchange gases
Action of pulling air into the lungs
Action of pushing waste gas out of the lungs

A.explain: Trachea is the long tube that takes air from the mouth to the bronchi. Diaphragm is the flat muscle that pulls and pushes the lungs. Alveoli are tiny air sacs with thin walls to exchange gases. Inhale is the action of pulling air into the lungs. Exhale is the action of pushing waste gas out of the lungs. Storing food fits none of these.

A.q: Oxygen is the gas from the air we mix with nutrients to make what?
A.explain: Oxygen from air mixes with nutrients to make energy. Feces and bile are waste or digestive fluids, and carbon dioxide is an exhaled waste gas; none is the energy product.

A.q: Carbon dioxide is described as what?
A.explain: Carbon dioxide is the waste gas exhaled by the body. Nutrient gas, carrier gas, and inert gas do not match the description.

A.q: Bronchi and bronchioles are tubes that take air into the lungs and remove which gas?
A.explain: Bronchi and bronchioles take air into the lungs and remove carbon dioxide. Oxygen, nitrogen, and water vapor do not match the removal described.

A.q: Capillaries are fine tubes that carry blood to and from what?
A.explain: Capillaries are fine tubes that carry blood to and from cells. The heart, the lungs, and the stomach are not the exchange sites described.

A.q: What is the primary purpose of the heart?
options: It pumps blood to supply cell needs
It filters blood to remove waste
It stores oxygen for the cells
A.explain: The heart pumps life-giving blood throughout the body so cells receive their needs. It works with blood and blood vessels. Filtering waste, producing plasma, and storing oxygen are not its primary purpose.

A.q: An artery is a blood vessel that carries blood in which direction?
A.explain: An artery carries blood away from the heart. A vein carries blood back toward the heart.

A.q: A valve in each ventricle stops blood from flowing where?
A.explain: A valve in each ventricle stops the blood from flowing backwards. Forwards, sideways, and upward do not describe the prevention stated.

A.q: Plasma makes up over half of the blood and helps regulate what?
A.explain: Plasma makes up over half of the blood and helps regulate body temperature. Bone density, heart rate, and oxygen levels are not the regulation stated for plasma.

A.q: Which statement about veins is correct?
options: Veins carry blood back to the heart
Veins carry blood away from the heart
Veins have thicker walls than arteries
A.explain: Veins carry blood back to the heart. Their walls are thinner than arteries, and skin veins may look blue. Arteries carry blood away; thicker walls and oxygen-only blood are false.

A.q: Which of the following is not true?
options: Blood flows at the same speed through the entire body
The heart is located a little to the left of the center of the chest
Veins carry blood back to the heart
The heart beats every second of the day
A.explain: Blood does not flow at the same speed throughout the entire body. As it gets farther away from the heart, it slows down. The heart is located a little to the left of the center of the chest. Veins carry blood back to the heart. The heart beats continuously.

A.q: What makes up over one-half of our blood?
A.explain: Plasma makes up over half of the blood. Red cells, white cells, and platelets float in the plasma but do not make up over half by themselves.

A.q: Veins on the skin are especially visible on the hands and arms. Which description matches?
A.explain: Veins on the skin may look blue, especially on the hands and arms. Slightly pink, big and bulgy, and gray do not match the description.

A.q: The body uses nutrients for energy, growth, and what?
A.explain: The body uses nutrients for energy, growth, and tissue repair. Gas exchange, bile storage, and waste filtration are not the primary uses stated for nutrients.

A.q: Nutrients are absorbed into the blood through tiny pores in which structures of the small intestine?
A.explain: These are absorbed into the blood through tiny pores in the villi, the fronds that project from the intestinal wall. Alveoli, bronchi, and capillaries only are not the structures named for this absorption.

A.q: Hunger pangs occur when the body needs food or expects a routine meal; appetite is a pleasurable sensation from digestive juices in the mouth and stomach. What do hunger pangs result from?
A.explain: Hunger pangs result from stomach contractions driven by the nervous and hormonal systems. Breathing patterns move air, while heartbeat rhythms and pulse measurements track the heart; none cause hunger pangs.

A.q: During inhalation, what does the nose do to the air?
A.explain: During inhalation the nose cleans, warms, and moistens the air. Filtering and cooling, heating and blocking, or moistening and cooling do not match the described function.

A.q: The heart is located in the middle of the chest and slightly to the left. Blood from the ventricles goes to the lungs and to every cell. Which statement aligns?
options: Blood enters the upper atria first, then the lower ventricles.
Blood enters the lower ventricles first, then the upper atria.
The heart lies entirely on the right side of the chest.
The ventricles send blood only to the lungs, not cells.
A.explain: Blood enters the upper atria, then the lower ventricles. The heart is mid-chest, slightly left. Ventricles send blood to the lungs and every cell. Valves stop blood flowing backwards.

A.q: A main artery may be as thick as what?
A.explain: A main artery can be as thick as a thumb. A finger, a hair, and a capillary are all narrower and do not match the comparison.

A.q: The Superior Vena Cava and Inferior Vena Cava return blood to the heart. Which regions do they drain?
options: Brain and chest; stomach and lower body
Brain and chest; arms and legs
Stomach and lower body; heart and lungs
Arms and legs; brain and chest
A.explain: The Superior Vena Cava drains the brain and chest; the Inferior Vena Cava drains the stomach and lower body. These two large veins return blood to the heart. The other pairs misassign these regions.

A.q: The heart beats or pumps 100,000 times a day. The pulse can be felt on the inside of the wrist. What is the adult pulse rate?
A.explain: Adults are 60 to 100 beats per minute; children are 90 to 120. The heart beats about 100,000 times a day, and the pulse is felt inside the wrist.

A.q: In an average person's lifetime, the digestive system processes about how much food?
A.explain: In an average person's lifetime, the digestive system processes 30,000 kg (66,000 lb) of food. The smaller amounts do not match the stated figure.

A.q: What propels food through the digestive tract?
options: Muscular contractions in the tract wall
Skeletal support from the vertebral column
Blood pressure within the circulatory loop
A.explain: Food is propelled by muscular contractions in the tract wall. 'Skeletal support from the vertebral column' holds body shape. 'Blood pressure within the circulatory loop' moves blood. 'Airflow through the nasal passage' moves air.

A.q: Which tube extends from the mouth to the anus and contains hollow organs?
A.explain: The digestive tract extends from the mouth to the anus and includes hollow organs such as the stomach and intestines. 'The respiratory tract' carries air. 'The circulatory loop' carries blood. 'The skeletal axis' supports the body.

A.q: Select all associated organs of the digestive system.
A.explain: The salivary glands, the liver, and the pancreas are associated digestive organs. The stomach is part of the digestive tract.

A.q: Why must most food molecules be broken down before absorption?
options: They are too large to cross cell membranes
They are too watery to enter blood vessels
They are too gaseous to reach lung alveoli
They are too mineralized to form bone tissue
A.explain: Most food molecules are too large to cross cell membranes, so they must be broken down before absorption. 'They are too watery to enter blood vessels' is not the reason. 'They are too gaseous to reach lung alveoli' describes air exchange. 'They are too mineralized to form bone tissue' describes bone formation.

A.q: What do enzymes in digestive juices do?
A.explain: Enzymes in digestive juices speed up chemical reactions. 'Moisten food for swallowing' is a saliva function. 'Emulsify fat for absorption' is a bile function. 'Store bile until digestion' is a gallbladder function.

A.q: What do digestive acids help convert large molecules into?
A.explain: Digestive acids help convert large molecules into small absorbable units. 'Thick intestinal gases' are waste gas. 'Undigested food bolus' is the mouth mass. 'Semi-liquid stomach chyme' is the stomach mixture.

A.q: Why does chewing help enzyme action in digestion?
options: It exposes a large surface area
A.explain: Chewing breaks food into small particles and exposes a large surface area. 'It moistens food for swallowing' is a saliva function. 'It emulsifies fat for absorption' is a bile function. 'It stores bile until digestion' is a gallbladder function.

A.q: After absorption, blood carries nutrients to which organ before body cells?
A.explain: After absorption, blood carries nutrients to the liver, then to the body cells. 'The gallbladder' stores bile. 'The pancreas' produces pancreatic juice. 'The rectum' collects feces.

A.q: Which systems ensure digestive juices are secreted at the right time and control muscular walls?
A.explain: Nervous and hormonal systems ensure digestive juices are secreted at the right time and control muscular walls. 'Cardiovascular and respiratory systems' move blood and air. 'Skeletal and integumentary systems' support and protect. 'Lymphatic and urinary systems' handle tissue fluid and waste.

A.q: What do local glands release when food enters the stomach or intestines?
options: Hormones that activate digestive juice production
Bile that emulsifies dietary fat for absorption
Saliva that moistens food for chewing and swallowing
Lymph that returns tissue fluid to the blood
A.explain: Local glands release hormones that activate digestive juice production when food enters the stomach or intestines. 'Bile that emulsifies dietary fat for absorption' relates to fat digestion. 'Saliva that moistens food for chewing and swallowing' begins digestion in the mouth. 'Lymph that returns tissue fluid to the blood' is not a digestive secretion.

A.q: What determines how much and how often a person eats?
A.explain: Hunger and appetite determine how much and how often a person eats. 'Pulse and respiration' are vital signs. 'Body temperature and blood pressure' are regulatory measurements. 'Collagen and minerals' are structural substances.

A.q: Match each trigger to the response it stimulates.
A.explain: Low blood sugar, Empty stomach, and Regular meal time stimulate Hunger. Sight of food and Smell of food stimulate Appetite. Thirst is a drive for water and fits none of these triggers.

A.q: What do the esophagus and stomach allow a person to do?
options: Swallow a large amount quickly and digest it at leisure
Absorb nutrients directly through the small intestinal wall
Secrete bile before food enters the mouth or stomach
Expel feces without muscular contractions in the tract
A.explain: The esophagus and stomach allow a person to swallow a large amount quickly and digest it at leisure. 'Absorb nutrients directly through the small intestinal wall' is a small-intestine function. 'Secrete bile before food enters the mouth or stomach' is not an esophagus or stomach function. 'Expel feces without muscular contractions in the tract' contradicts muscular propulsion.

A.q: Which structure is the largest internal organ of the body?
A.explain: The liver is the largest internal organ. 'The trachea' is the windpipe of the airway. 'The esophagus' is the muscular food tube. 'The stomach' stores and churns food but is smaller than the liver.

A.q: About how long does food remain in the stomach before passing to the small intestine?
A.explain: Food stays about 5 hours in the stomach. 'About 15 hours' and 'About 50 hours' overstate the gastric phase. 'About 5 minutes' is far too brief for digestion in the stomach.

A.q: Which structure is commonly called the throat?
A.explain: The pharynx is the structure commonly called the throat. 'The trachea' is the windpipe. 'The esophagus' is the food pipe. 'The stomach' is the abdominal storage bag.

A.q: The upper end of the oesophagus stays closed except during which action?
A.explain: The upper oesophagus opens only when swallowing a bolus. 'Breathing in fresh air' keeps it shut, since air travels through the trachea. 'Secreting gastric acid' occurs in the stomach. 'Circulating oxygenated blood' is a heart and vessel function.

A.q: What shape is the stomach described as?
A.explain: The stomach is a J-shaped bag. 'A S-shaped tube' matches no digestive organ here. 'A perfectly round sac' misstates the curvature. 'A thin flattened disc' misstates both the shape and the thickness.

A.q: How many liters of gastric juice does the stomach secrete?
A.explain: The stomach secretes about 3 liters of gastric juice. 'About 13 liters', 'About 30 liters', and 'About 300 liters' all overstate the gastric volume.

A.q: The small intestine connects the stomach to which structure?
A.explain: The small intestine links the stomach to the large intestine. 'The muscular esophagus' lies above the stomach. 'The terminal rectum' and 'The distal anal canal' lie beyond the large intestine.

A.q: The heart ___ about 14,000 liters of blood around the body each day.
A.explain: The heart pumps about 14,000 liters of blood daily. 'stimulates' means triggering activity, not moving a volume. 'vaccinates' means giving immunity. 'flows' is intransitive and cannot take the blood volume as its object.

A.q: The heart is ___ of four chambers, two atria and two ventricles.
A.explain: The heart is composed of four chambers. 'eradicated' means wiped out. 'eliminated' means removed. 'consisted' cannot follow 'is'; the correct form is 'consists of'.

A.q: Capillaries are responsible for the ___ of nutrients and waste between cells and blood.
A.explain: Capillaries handle the exchange of nutrients and waste. 'exposure' means contact without transfer. 'secretion' means producing and releasing a substance. 'filtration' means straining fluid, not the two-way swap capillaries perform.

A.q: In 'the digestive tract extends from the mouth to the anus', what does 'extends' mean?
A.explain: 'extends' means spreads over a distance. 'shortens' and 'decreases' express reduction. 'contracts' expresses drawing inward.

A.q: In 'the system [[extracts]] nutrients and [[disposes]] of waste', what do the underlined words mean?
A.explain: 'extracts' means takes out and 'disposes' means gets rid of. 'removes / retains within' is right on the first word but wrong on the second, since retaining opposes disposing. 'utilizes / remains upon' mismatches both. 'inserts / discards away' reverses the first word.

A.q: In 'enzymes [[convert]] large molecules into [[absorbable]] units', what do the underlined words mean?
options: Alter / Able to be taken in
A.explain: 'convert' means alter and 'absorbable' means able to be taken in. 'change / capable of replacement' is close on the first but wrong on the second. 'alter / having resistance power' mismatches the second. 'retain / capable of being taken' mismatches the first.

A.q: In 'chewing breaks food into particles', what does 'particles' mean?
A.explain: 'Particles' means small bits or pieces. 'large units or blocks' and 'huge parts or wholes' state the opposite size. 'whole objects or masses' denies the broken-up sense.

A.q: In 'organs secrete juices that aid digestion', what does 'secrete' mean?
A.explain: 'Secrete' means produce or discharge. 'absorb or take in fully' is the opposite uptake. 'expose openly to view' means revealing, not releasing fluid. 'destroy or break down' describes enzymatic action, not glandular release.

A.q: Blood is ___ for body functioning as it ___ oxygen to the body parts.
A.explain: Blood is essential and it transports oxygen. 'significant / avoids' is wrong on the second verb. 'quite simple / implants' is wrong on both. 'very complex / resists' is wrong on the second verb.

A.q: The digestive tract is about how long?
A.explain: The digestive tract is about 7 m long. The small intestine is about 5 m, and the large intestine is about 1.5 m.

A.q: Which folded membrane covers and secures the digestive organs?
A.explain: The peritoneum is the folded membrane that covers and secures the digestive organs. The pericardium surrounds the heart, the pleura covers the lungs, and the meninges cover the brain and spinal cord.

A.q: The wave of muscle contractions that moves food along the tract is called ___.
A.explain: Peristalsis is the sequence of muscle contractions that propels food through the digestive tract. Absorption moves nutrients into the blood, secretion releases juices, and digestion breaks down food.

A.q: The large intestine includes the caecum, the colon, and the ___.
A.explain: The large intestine includes the caecum, colon, and rectum. The stomach and esophagus are upper digestive tract organs, and the spleen is not part of the digestive tract.

A.q: Food can take how long to pass through the digestive tract?
A.explain: Food can take many hours to pass through the digestive tract. It is not digested instantly.

A.q: The digestive system can process a variety of diets, such as meat-based diets and diets mainly of ___.
A.explain: The digestive system processes both meat-based diets and plant-based diets such as rice and fish. Bread and salt is too limited, sugar and fat is unbalanced, and water and air are not food.

A.q: The heart is located in the middle of the chest and slightly to the ___.
A.explain: The heart is located in the middle of the chest and slightly to the left.

A.q: Red blood cells carry oxygen and ___ to the cells.
A.explain: Red blood cells carry oxygen and food/nutrients to the cells. Bile, urine, and saliva are not carried by red blood cells to body cells.

A.q: Plasma carries nutrients from the stomach to be used as fuel for ___.
A.explain: Plasma carries nutrients from the stomach to be used as fuel for energy. Oxygen, waste, and bile are not what the nutrients are used as fuel for.

A.q: Blood is made of red cells, white cells, platelets, and ___.
A.explain: Blood is made of red cells, white cells, and platelets floating in plasma. Bile is digestive, chyme is stomach contents, and lymph belongs to the lymphatic system.

A.q: Besides the nose, which opening can let air enter the respiratory system?
A.explain: Air can enter the respiratory system through the mouth and the nose. The stomach, liver, and kidney are not openings for inhaled air.

A.q: The larynx is also called the ___.
A.explain: The larynx is the voice box. It helps us speak and make sounds when air moves in and out. The windpipe is the trachea, the throat is the pharynx, and air sacs are alveoli.

A.q: Which structure carries air from the mouth and nose to the trachea?
A.explain: The pharynx, or throat, delivers air from the mouth and nose to the trachea. The esophagus carries food to the stomach, the bronchus leads into the lung, and the diaphragm is the breathing muscle.

A.q: The trachea is also called the ___.
A.explain: The trachea is the windpipe. It carries air between the throat and the lungs. The voice box is the larynx, the throat is the pharynx, and the lungs contain alveoli.

A.q: Which two main tubes branch from the trachea and lead into the lungs?
A.explain: The bronchi are the two main tubes from the trachea into the lungs. Alveoli are air sacs, capillaries are blood vessels, and bronchioles are the smaller branches, not the two main tubes.

A.q: What are bronchioles?
A.explain: Bronchioles are small branches of the bronchial tubes that lead to the alveoli. The alveoli are the tiny sacs where gas exchange happens, the diaphragm is the muscle below the lungs, and the ribs are bones around the chest.

A.q: Which organs remove oxygen from the air and pass it into the blood?
A.explain: The lungs are the two organs that remove oxygen from inhaled air and pass it into the blood. The liver processes substances, the kidneys filter blood, and the stomach digests food.

A.q: During ___, the nose cleans, warms, and moistens the air.
A.explain: Inhalation is the process of breathing in. During inhalation, the nose helps clean, warm, and moisten the air. Exhalation is breathing out, digestion breaks down food, and circulation moves blood.

A.q: The process of breathing out is called ___.
A.explain: Exhalation is the process of breathing out. Inhalation is breathing in, absorption is taking substances into the body or blood, and secretion is producing and releasing a substance.

A.q: Which bones surround and protect the lungs and heart?
A.explain: The ribs form the rib cage around the chest and help protect the lungs and heart. Vertebrae form the spine, the pelvis is at the base of the trunk, and the clavicles are collarbones.

A.q: In respiratory vocabulary, the nasal cavity is another name for the ___.
A.explain: The nasal cavity is the space inside the nose. The throat is the pharynx, the voice box is the larynx, and the windpipe is the trachea.

A.q: How many hours does it take to churn food into a pulp?
A.explain: Food is typically churned in the stomach for about 2–4 hours and turned into semi-liquid chyme before gradual release into the small intestine. About 4 hours is the standard figure for a typical mixed meal. About 5 hours fits larger or high-fat meals. About 6 hours is long for most meals, and about 3 hours is on the shorter side for complete processing of solid food.

A.q: About how long does food typically remain in the stomach during digestion?
A.explain: Food typically remains in the stomach for about 5 hours during digestion before passing into the small intestine. About 2 hours and about 3 hours are shorter than usual for a typical mixed meal. About 8 hours is longer than normal gastric processing time.
